messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Akua had always taken pride in his role as a school principal, but it was a crisp autumn evening, six months ago, that changed everything. He had stopped at a local bar after work to catch up with some colleagues when he was assaulted by a stranger who had been drinking heavily. The smell of alcohol still lingered on the man's breath as he pinned Akua against the wall, leaving him feeling helpless and terrified. As the attacker's grip tightened around his wrist, Akua felt an overwhelming sense of loss of control, as if his entire body was frozen in place. Since that night, the scent of alcohol has become a potent trigger for Akua. Whenever he catches a whiff of it, he is instantly transported back to that moment of utter powerlessness. His mind begins to scan the surroundings, searching for potential escape routes and exits – a habit that has become second nature whenever he enters a new room or building. This hypervigilance leaves him feeling jumpy and on edge, as if even the slightest unexpected movement might signal another attack. As Akua navigates his daily routine, these triggers inevitably lead to memories of that fateful night. The sound of shattering glass still echoes in his mind, a haunting auditory recall that makes him feel like he's reliving the trauma all over again. When these memories surface, Akua often feels a deep sense of grief wash over him, as if he's mourning the loss of some fundamental aspect of himself. Other times, however, he experiences an eerie numbness – a disconnection from his own emotions that makes it feel like the event happened to someone else entirely. Akua has come to believe that this lack of control and autonomy during the assault has left him with a crippling sense of self-doubt. He can't shake the feeling that if only he had acted differently, the attack might have been avoided. This self-blame seeps into every aspect of his life, making it difficult for him to trust either himself or others. His relationships begin to suffer as a result – his wife feels like she's walking on eggshells around him, never knowing when some small trigger will set off another emotional avalanche. As Akua struggles to make sense of these emotions, he finds himself increasingly trapped in a cycle of threat and avoidance. His constant scanning for exits becomes an exhausting task, leaving him feeling drained and anxious even in the safety of his own home. This perceived threat also reinforces his negative appraisals – if he can't rely on himself or others to keep him safe, then what's the point of trying at all? The memories of that night continue to haunt him, a constant reminder of his own vulnerability. It was this suffocating cycle that finally brought Akua to seek help. His wife staged an intervention, pointing out how his avoidance behaviors were taking a toll on their relationship and his job as principal. As he sat in the therapist's office, surrounded by the familiar scent of books and coffee, Akua felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, there was a way to break free from this cycle of pain and reclaim some semblance of control over his life. Akua is afraid that therapy won't be enough, that he'll never be able to shake off the lingering memories of that night. But more than anything, he hopes to rediscover the sense of autonomy and self-worth that was taken from him in that moment – to learn how to trust himself and others once again, and find a way to live with the scars of his past without being forever trapped by them.
